body_markdown:
Few brands and models have the cachet of Shelby and the Cobra. And while every Cobra comes packed with a story, some are a little more interesting and varied than others. Given that this particular Cobra is noted in The World Registry of Cobras and GT40s as “the only 427 Cobra prototype,” chassis number CSX2196 might well be among the most special Cobras to leave the shop—or at least it’s the easiest to take apart.


This rare look not only at but into the car comes via Peter Klutt and Legendary Motorcar on YouTube. The car’s storied history starts as a small-block 289 car that was on the receiving end of a big-block 427 swap before racing at Sebring in 1964. It didn’t work out well, but the team saw potential in what had become known as “the turd” and used it as a test bed, revising the car regularly to hone the platform for big-block use. When done, it became known as the “Flip-Top.”


The whole body comes off with a number of[Dzus fasteners](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/hail-dzus-connector-of-race-car-and-motorcycle-parts/) , and that is when the cool kit really starts to appear. Klutt breaks down all the details, from the revised frame and bracing to the adjustable lower control arms that were fabricated by Ken Miles himself. The rest of the chassis is equally fascinating and includes noticeable differences and special bits down to the aircraft hardware and brake calipers that are still stamped with the original production dates of the early 1960s.


Chassis 2196 weighs in at only about 1800 pounds, and, equipped with an experimental 390-cubic-inch FE motor, duked it out with the Corvette Grand Sports at Nassau Speed Week at the end of 1964. It jumped out to a healthy lead before the engine gave up. In the Registry, Ted Sutton, the Shelby mechanic initially responsible for the car, is quoted about 2196: “Lots of skepticism went along with this … Making a big snake out of a little one wasn’t the ideal way to go racing. But the concept needed a beginning and you had to start somewhere.”


Legendary Motorcars


Legendary Motorcars


Given its experimental history and unique construction, there’s no other Cobra like 2196. That makes it a bit of a challenge to understand what it’s worth. “The current high-water mark overall is the[$42.9M](https://www.goodingco.com/lot/1964-shelby-cobra-daytona-coupe) Daytona Coupe sold earlier this year, and for Cobra roadsters it’s CSX2000 (the very first Cobra), which sold 10 years ago for[$13.75M](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mo16/lots/r193-1962-shelby-260-cobra-csx-2000/) ,” explains senior auction editor Andrew Newton. “There’s also Carroll Shelby’s personal Cobra (which sold for[$5.94M](https://www.mecum.com/lots/444471/1965-shelby-427-cobra-roadster/) in 2021) and the famous Super Snake (sold for[$5.5M](https://www.barrett-jackson.com/scottsdale-march-2021/docket/vehicle/1966-shelby-cobra-427-super-snake-245431) in 2021). The Flip-Top Cobra arguably falls behind all of those given its lack of real racing success, but mid-seven-figures seems reasonable given its part its level of preservation, unique configuration, role in big-block Cobra development, and the Ken Miles connection.”


While it might not be the most valuable, the Flip-Top is definitely in the running for one of the coolest and historically relevant Cobras out there. And we can’t get enough of watching it come apart and go back together so easily.
